verses.zh: 第十一年十一月初一日，耶和华的话临到我说：
verses.en: In the eleventh year, on the first day of the month,[NOTE:1] the Lord’s message came to me:
notes: April 23, 587 b.c. tc Date formulae typically include the month. According to D. I. Block (Ezekiel [NICOT], 2:34, n. 27) some emend to “in the twelfth year in the eleventh month,” relying partially on the copy of the LXX from Alexandrinus, where Albright suggested that “eleventh month” may have dropped out due to haplography.

verses.zh: 「人子啊，因泰尔向耶路撒冷说：『阿哈，那作众民之门的已经破坏，向我开放；她既变为荒场，我必丰盛。』
verses.en: “Son of man, because Tyre[NOTE:1] has said about Jerusalem,[NOTE:2] ‘Aha, the gateway of the peoples is broken; it has swung open to me. I will become rich,[NOTE:3] now that she[NOTE:4] has been destroyed,’
notes: Tyre was located on the Mediterranean coast north of Israel.
For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.
Heb “I will be filled.”
That is, Jerusalem.

verses.zh: 所以，主耶和华如此说：泰尔啊，我必与你为敌，使许多国民上来攻击你，如同海使波浪涌上来一样。
verses.en: therefore this is what the Sovereign Lord says: Look,[NOTE:1] I am against you,[NOTE:2] O Tyre! I will bring up many nations against you, as the sea brings up its waves.
notes: The word הִנֵּה (hinneh, traditionally “behold”) draws attention to something and has been translated here as a verb.

Or “I challenge you.” The phrase “I am against you” may be a formula for challenging someone to combat or a duel. See D. I. Block, Ezekiel (NICOT), 1:201-2, and P. Humbert, “Die Herausforderungsformel ‘hinnenî ’êlékâ’” ZAW 45 (1933): 101-8.

verses.zh: 他们必破坏泰尔的墙垣，拆毁她的城楼。我也要刮净尘土，使她成为净光的磐石。
verses.en: They will destroy the walls of Tyre and break down her towers. I will scrape her soil[NOTE:1] from her and make her a bare rock.
notes: Or “debris.”

verses.zh: 她必在海中作晒网的地方，也必成为列国的掳物。这是主耶和华说的。
verses.en: She will be a place where fishing nets are spread, surrounded by the sea. For I have spoken, declares the Sovereign Lord. She will become plunder for the nations,

verses.zh: 属泰尔城邑的居民（原文是田间的众女；八节同）必被刀剑杀灭，他们就知道我是耶和华。
verses.en: and her daughters[NOTE:1] who are in the field will be slaughtered by the sword. Then they will know that I am the Lord.
notes: That is, the towns located inland that were under Tyre’s rule.

verses.zh: 主耶和华如此说：「我必使诸王之王的巴比伦王尼布甲尼撒率领马匹车辆、马兵、军队，和许多人民从北方来攻击你泰尔。
verses.en: “For this is what the Sovereign Lord says: Take note that[NOTE:1] I am about to bring King Nebuchadrezzar[NOTE:2] of Babylon, king of kings, against Tyre from the north, with horses, chariots, and horsemen, an army and hordes of people.
notes: The word הִנֵּה (hinneh, traditionally “behold”) draws attention to something.
Heb “Nebuchadrezzar” is a variant and more correct spelling of Nebuchadnezzar, as the Babylonian name Nabu-kudurri-uṣur has an “r” rather than an “n.”

verses.zh: 他必用刀剑杀灭属你城邑的居民，也必造台筑垒举盾牌攻击你。
verses.en: He will kill your daughters in the field with the sword. He will build a siege wall against you, erect a siege ramp against you, and raise a great shield against you.

verses.zh: 他必安设撞城锤攻破你的墙垣，用铁器拆毁你的城楼。
verses.en: He will direct the blows of his battering rams against your walls and tear down your towers with his weapons.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “swords.”

verses.zh: 因他的马匹众多，尘土扬起遮蔽你。他进入你的城门，好像人进入已有破口之城。那时，你的墙垣必因骑马的和战车、辎重车的响声震动。
verses.en: He will cover you with the dust kicked up by his many horses.[NOTE:1] Your walls will shake from the noise of the horsemen, wheels, and chariots when he enters your gates like those who invade through a city’s broken walls.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “From the abundance of his horses he will cover you (with) their dust.”
Heb “like those who enter a breached city.”

verses.zh: 他的马蹄必践踏你一切的街道，他必用刀杀戮你的居民；你坚固的柱子（或译：柱像）必倒在地上。
verses.en: With his horses’ hooves he will trample all your streets. He will kill your people with the sword, and your strong pillars will tumble down to the ground.

verses.zh: 人必以你的财宝为掳物，以你的货财为掠物，破坏你的墙垣，拆毁你华美的房屋，将你的石头、木头、尘土都抛在水中。
verses.en: They will steal your wealth and loot your merchandise. They will tear down your walls and destroy your luxurious[NOTE:1] homes. Your stones, your trees, and your soil he will throw[NOTE:2] into the water.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “desirable.”
Heb “set.”
Heb “into the midst of the water.”

verses.zh: 我必使你唱歌的声音止息，人也不再听见你弹琴的声音。
verses.en: I will silence[NOTE:1] the noise of your songs; the sound of your harps will be heard no more.
notes: Heb “cause to end.”

verses.zh: 我必使你成为净光的磐石，作晒网的地方；你不得再被建造，因为这是主耶和华说的。」
verses.en: I will make you a bare rock; you will be a place where fishing nets are spread. You will never be built again,[NOTE:1] for I, the Lord, have spoken, declares the Sovereign Lord.
notes: This prophecy was fulfilled by Alexander the Great in 332 b.c.

verses.zh: 主耶和华对泰尔如此说：「在你中间行杀戮，受伤之人唉哼的时候，因你倾倒的响声，海岛岂不都震动吗？
verses.en: “This is what the Sovereign Lord says to Tyre: Oh, how the coastlands will shake at the sound of your fall, when the wounded groan at the massive slaughter in your midst!

verses.zh: 那时靠海的君王必都下位，除去朝服，脱下花衣，披上战兢，坐在地上，时刻发抖，为你惊骇。
verses.en: All the princes of the sea will vacate[NOTE:1] their thrones. They will remove their robes and strip off their embroidered clothes; they will clothe themselves with trembling. They will sit on the ground; they will tremble continually and be shocked at what has happened to you.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “descend from.”
Heb “and they will be astonished over you.”

verses.zh: 他们必为你作起哀歌说：你这有名之城，素为航海之人居住，在海上为最坚固的；平日你和居民使一切住在那里的人无不惊恐；现在何竟毁灭了？
verses.en: They will sing this lament over you:[NOTE:1] “‘How you have perished—you have vanished[NOTE:2] from the seas,O renowned city, once mighty in the sea,she and her inhabitants, who spread their terror![NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “and they will lift up over you a lament and they will say to you.”

Heb “O inhabitant.” The translation follows the LXX and understands a different Hebrew verb, meaning “cease,” behind the consonantal text. See L. C. Allen, Ezekiel [WBC], 2:72, and D. I. Block, Ezekiel (NICOT), 2:43.

Heb “she and her inhabitants who placed their terror to all her inhabitants.” The relationship of the final prepositional phrase to what precedes is unclear. The preposition probably has a specifying function here, drawing attention to Tyre’s inhabitants as the source of the terror mentioned prior to this. In this case, one might paraphrase verse 17b: “she and her inhabitants, who spread their terror; yes, her inhabitants (were the source of this terror).”

verses.zh: 如今在你这倾覆的日子，海岛都必战兢；海中的群岛见你归于无有就都惊惶。」
verses.en: Now the coastlands will tremble on the day of your fall; the coastlands by the sea will be terrified by your passing.’[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “from your going out.”

verses.zh: 主耶和华如此说：「泰尔啊，我使你变为荒凉，如无人居住的城邑；又使深水漫过你，大水淹没你。
verses.en: “For this is what the Sovereign Lord says: When I make you desolate like the uninhabited cities, when I bring up the deep over you and the surging[NOTE:1] waters overwhelm you,
notes: Heb “many.”

verses.zh: 那时，我要叫你下入阴府，与古时的人一同在地的深处、久已荒凉之地居住，使你不再有居民。我也要在活人之地显荣耀（我也……荣耀：或译在活人之地不再有荣耀）。
verses.en: then I will bring you down to bygone people,[NOTE:1] to be with those who descend to the Pit.[NOTE:2] I will make you live in the lower parts of the earth among[NOTE:3] the primeval ruins, with those who descend to the Pit, so that you will not be inhabited or stand[NOTE:4] in the land of the living.
notes: Heb “to the people of antiquity.”
Heb “like.” The translation assumes an emendation of the preposition כ (kaf, “like”) to ב (bet, “in, among”).

Heb “and I will place beauty.” This reading makes little sense; many, following the lead of the LXX, emend the text to read: “nor will you stand,” with the negative particle before the preceding verb understood by ellipsis; see L. C. Allen, Ezekiel (WBC), 2:73. D. I. Block (Ezekiel [NICOT], 2:47) offers another alternative, taking the apparent first person verb form as an archaic second feminine form and translating “nor radiate splendor.”

verses.zh: 我必叫你令人惊恐，不再存留于世；人虽寻找你，却永寻不见。这是主耶和华说的。」
verses.en: I will bring terrors on you, and you will be no more! Though you are sought after, you will never be found again, declares the Sovereign Lord.”

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible.
Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing
is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

- First paragraph

- Second paragraph

- Third paragraph, etc.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: EZEKIEL 26:1-6

1Now in the eleventh year, on the first of the month, the word of the Lord came
to me saying, 2"Son of man, because Tyre has said concerning Jerusalem, 'Aha, the gateway of the peoples is broken; it has opened to me. I shall be filled,
now that she is laid waste,' 3therefore thus says the Lord God, 'Behold, I am against you, O Tyre, and I will bring up many
nations against you, as the sea brings up its waves. 4They will destroy the walls of Tyre and break down her towers; and I will scrape her debris from her and make
her a bare rock. 5She will be a place for the spreading of nets in the midst of the sea, for I have spoken,' declares the Lord God, 'and
she will become spoil for the nations. 6Also her daughters who are on the mainland will be slain by the sword, and they will know that I am the Lord.'"

26:1 Ezekiel dates his prophecies (cf. Ezek. 1:1; 8:1; 20:1; 26:1; 29:1,17; 30:20; 31:1; 32:1,17; 33:21). Surprisingly, the
month is not named here. His book is not in chronological sequence, which implies an editor. It must be admitted that moderns do not know
how, who, or when the OT was complied and edited in its current form.

Ezekiel 26:1 through 28:19 forms a literary unit denoting Phoenicia's judgment and total destruction. See note at Ezek. 26:11!
The subdivisions are identified by the literary marker "the word of the Lord came to me saying" (cf. Ezek. 26:1; 27:1; 28:1,11).

26:2 "the gateway of the peoples is broken" There are two ways of understanding this phrase.

- It has to do with Phoenicia's territorial expansion because of Judah's destruction of Neo-Babylon (notice the last phrase of v. 2).

- Jerusalem is located on a major international highway between the powerful nation of Egypt and the powerful nations of Syria, Anatolia,
and Mesopotamia. Because of her strategic location, Judah charged a tax on all of the caravans who passed this way. Tyre, also a
commercial center, was glad that one more middleman was eliminated.

- It relates to the use of the phrase in Isa. 62:10, which denotes Jerusalem, and particularly the temple, as a universal access (i.e. highway) to the worship of YHWH.

▣ "I shall be filled" This VERB (BDB 569, KB 583, Niphal COHORTATIVE) expresses
the joy of the Phoenicians at the demise of Judah ("she is laid waste," BDB 351, KB 349, Hophal PERFECT). The VERB
stem implies it was permanent.

▣ "because Tyre has said" Chapters 26-28 form a literary unit of judgment (a funeral dirge, cf. Ezek. 19:1-14; 26:17-18;
27:2-9,25-36; 28:12-19; 32:2-8) against the Phoenician maritime cities of Tyre and Sidon (cf. Isa. 24; Jer. 47:4).

26:3 These nations who gloated over Judah's fall were judged by YHWH (e.g. Micah 4:11).

▣ "as the sea brings up its waves" This is a play on the fact that Tyre was an island fortress.
Most of the city was located on the mainland, but the citadel was located on a rocky island about one-quarter
mile off shore. During ancient times it proved to be one of the most impregnable fortresses in the Near East.

26:4 This is another reference to the island fortress (cf. Ezek. 26:17). The city was finally captured by
Alexander the Great in 332 B.C.

26:5 This curse is repeated in Ezek. 26:14. There were two types of fishing nets used.

- casting nets, 12:13; 32:3

- dragnets, 26:5,14; 47:10

26:6 "her daughters who are on the mainland" This refers to the part of the city which surrounded the harbor. Only the walled citadel
was on the island. It was the walls of the houses and buildings that Alexander used to build a causeway to the islands (cf. Ezek. 26:12).

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: EZEKIEL 26:7-14

7For thus says the Lord God, "Behold, I will bring upon Tyre from the north
Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, king of kings, with horses, chariots, cavalry and a great army. 8He will slay your daughters on the mainland with the sword;
and he will make siege walls against you, cast up a ramp against you and raise up a large shield against you. 9The blow of his battering rams he will direct against
your walls, and with his axes he will break down your towers. 10Because of the multitude of his horses, the dust raised by them will cover you; your walls
will shake at the noise of cavalry and wagons and chariots when he enters your gates as men enter a city that is breached. 11With the hoofs of his horses he will
trample all your streets. He will slay your people with the sword; and your strong pillars will come down to the ground. 12Also they will make a spoil of your riches
and a prey of your merchandise, break down your walls and destroy your pleasant houses, and throw your stones and your timbers and your debris into the water. 13So
I will silence the sound of your songs, and the sound of your harps will be heard no more. 14I will make you a bare rock; you will be a place for the spreading of nets.
You will be built no more, for I the Lord have spoken," declares the Lord God.

26:7 "I will bring upon Tyre" Notice the actions of Neo-Babylon's army are controlled by YHWH. Nebuchadnezzar II is His instrument.

Flavius Josephus mentions that Nebuchadnezzar II seized the island fortress for 13 years (586-573 B.C.)
without taking it, but that a treaty was made in which the royal family was exiled but not the king himself (see IVP Bible Background Commentary [OT], p. 712).

▣ "from the north" This compass direction became a proverb (e.g. Jer. 4:6; 6:1,22; 10:22; 13:20; 15:12; 46:20, 24) for evil
because this was the only land route for invasion from the Fertile Crescent empires (i.e. Assyria in Isa. 14:31; Neo-Babylon in Jer. 1:13-15).

▣ "Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon" This Neo-Babylon king's name is spelled in two ways.

- Nebuchadnezzar ‒ 2 Kgs. 24:1,10,11; 25:1,8,22; 1 Chr. 6:15;
2 Chr. 36:6,7,10,13; Ezra 1:7; 2:1; 5:12,14; 6:5; Neh. 7:6; twenty-seven times in Daniel

- Nebuchadrezzar ‒ thirty-seven times in Jeremiah, four in Ezekiel

▣ "kings of kings" This title reflects the conquests of the Neo-Babylon Empire under
Nebuchadnezzar II (cf. Jer. 27:6-7; Dan. 2:37). It was also later used of Artaxerxes, the Persian king in
Ezra 7:12. It came to be a title for the Messiah (cf. 1 Tim. 6:15; Rev. 19:16). A similar title was used
of YHWH in Deut. 10:17 and I Enoch 9:4. It is a phrase that emphasizes sovereignty!

Special Topic: OT Titles of the Special Coming One

▣ "a great army" The Neo-Babylonian army grew by including the defeated armies into their ranks as
mercenaries.

26:8 "siege walls against you, cast up a mound" This may refer to two separate siege tactics or just to one (cf. 2 Sam. 20:15;
2 Kgs. 19:32; Isa. 37:33; Jer. 6:6; Ezek. 4:2; 17:17; 21:22; 26:8). These ramps allowed soldiers and siege machines (i.e. battering ram, BDB 867)
to approach the stone walls of a city in order to loosen the lower foundation stones and cause the wall to fall.

▣ "raise up a large shield against you" This is a technical term (BDB 857, cf. 1 Kgs. 10:16) for
what was known as "the roof" of the siege machines, which was raised as a shield to protect the attacking soldiers from those defenders on
the walls of citadels. We know that Nebuchadnezzar II began this siege in 587 B.C., and it lasted until 574 B.C.
Nebuchadnezzar never defeated the main citadel (cf. Ezek. 29:18), but it apparently surrendered. There is no record of the city's capture in the Babylonian chronicles.

26:9 Nebuchadnezzar's siege machines never reached the island citadel of Tyre, but Alexander's did in 332 B.C.

▣ "blow of his battering rams" This is a rare term (BDB 562 II). In Num. 34:11 it is translated
"border" (KB 568 or "to run along beside"), but that meaning does not fit this text in Ezekiel.

26:10 Neo-Babylon learned the use of cavalry and chariot warfare from the Assyrians (i.e. Jer. 6:23).

Special Topic: Chariots

26:11-12 There is a switch from the PRONOUN "he" (Ezek. 26:11) to "they"
(Ezek. 26:12) in these verses. Some have assumed a theological significance that this refers to subsequent
besiegers of Tyre, like Alexander the Great, to whom the city fell in 332 B.C. See
Gleason L. Archer, Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties, pp. 276-278.

26:11 Some would read these words and assert that the Bible is in error at this point. We must remember
that prophecy is hyperbolic literary genre. The books that have really helped me in my understanding of both prophecy and apocalyptic literature are

- D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic

- G. B. Caird, The Language and Imagery of the Bible

▣ "your strong pillars" From the Greek historian, Heroditus (II. 44), we understand there were two famous obelisks in the
city of Tyre. One was gold and the other was emerald and they were dedicated to the god Melqart ("King of the City"), probably another
name for Ba'al, the fertility god of Canaan. The worship of this god was brought into Israel by Jezebel (cf. 1 Kgs. 16:21-32).

26:13 This is an idiomatic way of asserting their society will cease (i.e. Isa. 23:16; 24:8,9). Tyre
may have been renowned for her musicians (cf. Isa. 23:16).

26:14 "a place for the spreading of nets" The citadel will be so completely destroyed that it will only be
good for is drying fishermen's nets (cf. Ezek. 26:5). This was historically fulfilled in Alexander's conquest.

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: EZEKIEL 26:15-18

15Thus says the Lord God to Tyre, "Shall not the coastlands
shake at the sound of your fall when the wounded groan, when the slaughter occurs in your midst? 16Then all the princes of the sea will go down
from their thrones, remove their robes and strip off their embroidered garments. They will clothe themselves with trembling; they will sit on the ground, tremble every
moment and be appalled at you. 17They will take up a lamentation over you and say to you,

'How you have perished, O inhabited one,

From the seas, O renowned city,

Which was mighty on the sea,

She and her inhabitants,

Who imposed her terror

On all her inhabitants!

18Now the coastlands will tremble

On the day of your fall;

Yes, the coastlands which are by the sea

Will be terrified at your passing.'"

26:15 "groan" This VERB (BDB 60, KB 72) occurs three times in Ezekiel.

- 9:4, those who sigh and groan over Judah's sins

- 24:17, Ezekiel groans quietly over the death of his wife

- 26:15, the dying of Tyre groan loudly at their approaching death (cf. Job 24:12; Jer. 51:52; Ezek. 30:24).
It occurs only one other time in the OT, Jer. 51:52. The NOUN (BDB 60)
occurs in Ps. 12:5; 79:11; 102:20; Mal. 2:13.

26:16 "they will sit on the ground" This is a sign of mourning (e.g. Lam. 2:10, esp. for a king, cf.
Isa. 47:1).

Special Topic: Grieving Rites

▣ "trembling. . .tremble" This term (BDB 353, KB 350) denotes great fear. It is used
twice (VERB and NOUN) in this verse. The ones
trembling are the colonies which the Phoenicians had started all around the Mediterranean. These outposts
of Phoenician culture were dependant on Tyre.

▣ "be appalled at you" This VERB (BDB 1030, KB
1563, Qal PERFECT with waw) denotes astonishment at YHWH's
judgment (cf. Lev. 26:32; Job 17:8; Isa. 52:14; Jer. 50:13; Ezek. 26:16; 27:35; 28:19; 32:10; Dan. 8:27).
This fear at the fall of a powerful commercial nation is used in Revelation 18.

26:17-18 This is a lamentation (BDB 884, cf. Ezek. 2:10; 19:1,14; 27:2,32; 32:2,16) in poetic form.

26:17 The questions about the first two lines of the lament are:

- are there two parallel VERBALS

- "perished"

- "ceased" (NET Bible)

- are there two parallel titles

- O inhabited one

- O renewed city

- or, is there one of each

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: EZEKIEL 26:19-21

19For thus says the Lord God, "When I make you a desolate
city, like the cities which are not inhabited, when I bring up the deep over you and the great waters cover you, 20then I will bring you down with
those who go down to the pit, to the people of old, and I will make you dwell in the lower parts of the earth, like the ancient waste places, with those who go down
to the pit, so that you will not be inhabited; but I will set glory in the land of the living. 21I will bring terrors on you and you will be no more; though you
will be sought, you will never be found again," declares the Lord God.

26:19 "the deep over you and the great waters" This refers to the chaotic waters of creation (cf. Gen. 1:2,6-7,9-10), which became known as
Sheol or the holding place of the dead (i.e. "the pit," Ezek. 26:20; 31:16; Ps. 28:1; 30:3; 40:2; 88:4; 143:7; Prov. 1:12; Isa. 14:15; 38:18).

"The deep" is the Hebrew term tehom (BDB 1062 #3, KB 1690-91). A similar, but different, Hebrew root is personified as
Tiamat in the Sumerian and Babylonian creation myths as the monster of chaos and the mother of the gods, wife of Apsu. She tried to kill all lesser
gods that came forth from her.

Marduk killed her. Out of her body Marduk fashioned heaven and earth in the Babylonian Genesis account called Enuma Elish.

The Hebrews believed that water was the beginning element of creation (cf. Ps. 24:1; 104:6; 2 Pet. 3:5). It is never said to have
been created. However, the Hebrew term is MASCULINE, not FEMININE and it is unrelated etymologically to Tiamat.

There are passages in the OT which describe YHWH in conflict with personified watery chaos (cf. Ps. 74:13-14; 89:9-10; 104:6-7;
Isa. 51:9-10). However, these are always in poetical, metaphorical passages. Water is a crucial aspect of creation (cf. Ezek. 1:2b,6-7), but its creation is never mentioned.

Special Topic: The Dead, Where Are They?, I. B.

26:20 "I shall bring you down with those who go down to the pit" This refers to Sheol, the holding place of the dead
until judgment day. The rabbis speculated that it was divided into two sections—the righteous dead and the wicked dead.

This three-level worldview (earth for the living, below the earth for the dead, and heaven above, e.g. Ps. 139:8; Amos 9:2)
was based on the burial practice of the Jews. The dead were buried, so they were in the ground (cf. Ezek. 31:14,16,18; 32:18,24). Smoke
from the sacrifices and incense altars rose to God so heaven was up. This is metaphorical, not literal (e.g. Isa. 14:9-10). In reality Scripture
reveals very little about the afterlife (heaven or hell), but focuses on choices, actions, and consequences of current reality!
